newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - Hyder seeks operating cost cuts.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Hyder seeks operating cost cuts.

text.p: British multi-utility Hyder Plc is studying possibilities for cuts in operational costs from its merged water and electricity businesses which could entail job losses, finance director Paul Twamley told Reuters in a telephone interview.

"What we're trying to do now is to look to see whether there is a case for putting some of the operational activities together and I believe there is, in which case we will have another tranche of cost savings and merger savings coming through in the next couple of years," Twamley said.
"That will include job cuts," he said, but added these would be voluntary.
Twamley said Hyder did not yet have firm figures on the cost savings or job losses as it had just set up a team to consider the possibilities for operational savings.

He said cost savings in the group's merged services company along with other merger benefits were 35.7 million pounds for the year, ahead of a targeted 27 million, under plans to reach 75 million total savings by 2000.

Hyder, which was formed when Welsh Water took over South Wales Electricity (Swalec) more than a year ago, saw annual pretax profits jump to 208.2 million pounds from 112.9 million and paid out a total dividend of 43.9 pence, up from 38.7 pence.
Twamley said staffing levels had fallen to 5,050 by March 31, 1997 from 5,490 a year earlier and were expected to reach 4,590 by 1999 under existing cost cutting plans.

He said the company intended to increase investment in non-regulated infrastructure projects worldwide by more than 30 million pounds a year from current levels of 70 million but in relatively low-risk projects.
"We're looking for 15 percent post-tax real (rate of return on capital) on our portfolio," he added.
Twamley said Hyder was looking at a number of projects but were being "very choosy on the countries in which we're prepared to operate".
Hyder said in a statement with results that non-regulated activities turned in profit before interest of 32.6 million pounds in the year to March 31, equivalent to 11.5 percent of total.
Twamley said the 11 percent real dividend growth was considered sustainable although he warned that the company was not forecasting dividend growth or cover levels.
